reviews.title: Disappointing after almost a year of learning
reviews.text:
I've been using Duolingo to learn Portuguese for almost a year, and I'm extremely disappointed with my progress.

According to the app, I've learned over 1,200 words and spoken more than 26,000, yet I still struggle to remember basic everyday vocabulary, construct simple sentences and hold even the most basic conversation.

Duolingo focuses far too heavily on recognising words, selecting answers and completing repetitive exercises rather than teaching you how to actually communicate.

Even with the video conversation features, I don't feel I've been given the foundations needed to understand and respond naturally in real-life situations.

After nearly a year of consistent learning, I expected to be able to have at least a simple conversation in Portuguese without constantly relying on a translator.

Duolingo is good at keeping you coming back every day, but in my experience, **maintaining a streak is very different from learning to speak a language.**

I'm seriously questioning whether the time and money I've invested have been worthwhile.

reviews.title: Annual Auto-Renewal with Zero Recourse
reviews.text:
I have been a dedicated Duolingo user for years, maintaining a 1,759-day streak.

I fell for their persistent marketing and agreed to a free trial of the Super Duolingo Family Plan, intending to evaluate it and switch to an individual monthly plan. Unfortunately, I was auto-renewed me into an unexpected $143.99 annual charge. When I immediately canceled the auto-renewal and reached out right away to revert to a monthly plan or get a refund, I was denied.

Duolingo states only Apple can refund and Apple denies the refund (twice), and users are left trapped paying nearly $144 for an annual commitment they never wanted. 

Forcing the highest annual tier on users after a trial with zero flexibility, no prorating, and no customer service resolution isn't just bad business—it's taking money from people for a service they explicitly said they don't want and giving them zero way out. It feels like legal theft, especially for anyone who genuinely cannot afford an unexpected $144 charge.

Disappointing to see an app I loved for nearly 5 years prioritize billing traps over doing the right thing by their costumers.

reviews.text:
I used to love Duolingo, but the more they rely on AI translations the worse the accuracy of their product. I’ve now lost count of the number of times I’ve seen errors in their French course recently. They seem more concerned these days with giving out digital puzzle pieces than prioritising the accuracy of their teaching materials.

There’s no accountability or follow up when you report an error - no one contacts you, nothing even acknowledges on an automated basis that the error you reported was dealt with. There’s no way to actually put in free text describing the issue, so the most likely outcome is that simply nothing is done to pick up on errors.

I wish I didn’t feel this way over what used to be such a great product. Hopefully it’ll redeem itself in the future, as right now people who don’t know a language well are probably banking on the fact that what’s in Duolingo is accurate and is helping them, when in reality it’s teaching mistakes.

reviews.title: A Critical Report on the Limitations and Ineffectiveness of Duolingo as a Language-Learning System
reviews.text:
Executive Summary
Duolingo has become one of the most recognizable language-learning platforms in the world, largely because it makes language study accessible, inexpensive, visually appealing, and easy to incorporate into a daily routine. Its gamified lessons, streak system, experience points, leagues, hearts, rewards, and short exercises encourage users to return repeatedly. However, these strengths also reveal a fundamental problem: Duolingo is exceptionally good at encouraging users to use Duolingo, but considerably less successful as a complete system for developing genuine communicative competence.

The central criticism is not that Duolingo contains no useful educational material. It does. Vocabulary exposure, basic sentence construction, pronunciation practice, and repeated retrieval can all contribute to language learning. The problem is that these components are frequently presented within a framework that prioritizes completion, repetition, immediate feedback, and gamification over deeper linguistic understanding and spontaneous communication.

This creates a substantial distinction between performing well inside the Duolingo environment and being able to function effectively in the language outside it. reviews.text: Overall I really like this app but I’m becoming increasingly disgruntled. I pay for super and for the most part it’s great. It has flaws but I generally accept them as they’re outweighed by the benefits. Sometimes the English translations are wrong and I report them but I doubt they ever get acted on. Flash card frenzy is good for testing vocabulary but now they have made it ridiculous on the highest level by reducing time so that it’s impossible - I’m slick with all the words and used to be able to do do it but they’ve just cut 15 seconds off the time and it’s physically impossible to do no matter how fast you say the words. The ambiguity doesn’t help since different words sometimes have more than one meaning and it’ll only accept the one it wants to so you have to say all the words it might mean e.g. it might say “you”, which could mean singular you “tú”, formal you “usted” or plural you “ustedes”, so you have to say all 3 in quick succession trying to second guess which it wants. Similarly “watch” could mean “to watch” (mirar) or “wristwatch” (reloj) but it’s not clear and you waste time by saying both. Also there’s no way to flag incorrect flash cards - like “responisble” (sic), which is clearly misspelled. As with all apps that become popular I’m sure greed somewhere has something to do with it as they all succumb to money and cost cutting at the sacrifice of customer experience.

reviews.title: Match Madness
reviews.text:
I used to really enjoy Match Madness because it was a fun and effective way to test vocabulary, speed, and recall. Unfortunately, after the last 3-4 updates in about one month of time, the experience has become noticeably less enjoyable.
The main issue is the timing and synchronisation of the matching words. Even when you are selecting the correct words quickly, the corresponding options sometimes do not appear at the same pace. On some occasions, I have experienced a delay of nearly 2 seconds before the matching word appears. Since the game is time-limited to 1 minute 45 seconds and requires rapid responses, these delays can easily lead to mistakes and make the experience frustrating rather than challenging.
Match Madness was one of the best features of Duolingo for me, but currently it feels like a great feature has been compromised by the recent updates. I sincerely hope the timing and synchronisation issues can be addressed soon. If feature can not be made responsive and consistent, it may be better to reconsider or redesign the mode rather than leave it in its current state.
I genuinely enjoy Duolingo and hope the team will look into this. The best thing has gone bad- I really hope to see Match Madness brought back to its former quality. Hoping for the Best!

reviews.title: Add Malaysian

Although I understand you are looking for a wide range of languages and Malay is very similar to Indonesian which you already have, I still find it strange to not include it at all. First of all, the similarities between Malay and Indonesian might not be as big as you think, actually they have an almost 20% difference, much more than intermediate English and normal English. Also Malay is a widely spoken language, unlike Latin, it is an official language of three different countries: Malaysia, Brunei and Singapore, making it useful for international travel and overseas communication. Lastly, there are nearly 2.5 million Malaysian diaspora globally of who might be second or third generation in need of learning their cultural background and heritage, which a major part of would be the language, this would help them feel connected to their people across seas. Overall, I find it is a complete overstep to not include this language due to how it is widely spoken, the need for connection to culture and how it is not that similar to Indonesian. If you are still convinced (somehow) that 20% is not that much then just copy and paste

I’ve updated this review to giving one star.  I have done the same lesson 4 times today.  Each time it crashes on the last question the last one!).  Each time you lose energy and any bonus score time you may have.  This app is getting worse not better.  

Original review:
When it is working it is good but it is very unreliable.  I have been using Duolingo everyday for about 300 days and LingoDeer for 100.  I ended up purchasing LingoDeer because the lessons are better and it just works.  Duolingo is fine, but there is too much focus on competing, and the app crashes at least once every day.  When it crashes during a lesson, you lose double/triple points time and, if you are using the free version, you loose energy and have to recharge before your next attempt.  When it crashes at the end of a lesson you often loose the achievements that lead to future doubling or tripling of points that you are forced to think about because of the competition.  It can be quite frustrating when you just want to do some lessons.    LingoDeer has better thought out lessons, the videos of real people make it much easier to pick up nuance, and although there is an element of competition, it’s not constantly rammed down your throat.  If you want free lessons and can put up with the glitches, Duolingo is fine, but if you want to pay for reliable language learning that feels properly thought through, there are other better options in my view.

reviews.title: IT'S REALLY BAD
reviews.text: Duolingo has become one of the most popular language-learning apps in the world, but many users argue that it falls short of being an effective way to achieve real fluency. Critics often point out that the app relies heavily on repetitive exercises that can feel more like a game than genuine language practice, causing learners to focus on earning points and maintaining streaks instead of developing meaningful communication skills. While the lessons may help beginners memorize vocabulary and basic sentence structures, they frequently lack the depth needed to understand complex grammar, natural conversation, regional expressions, and cultural context. Some users also find that the app’s artificial sentences and translation exercises do not accurately reflect how people speak in everyday situations. In addition, progress can sometimes feel misleading because completing lessons and advancing through levels may create the impression of significant improvement even when a learner struggles to hold a simple conversation with a native speaker. The increasing emphasis on premium features and subscriptions has also led some people to feel that the company prioritizes engagement and revenue over educational quality. As a result, many language learners view Duolingo as a useful supplement at best rather than a complete language-learning solution, arguing that real-world practice, conversation, reading, listening, and structured study are far more effective for achieving genuine proficien
